strengths: The survey addresses an important NLP problem: organizing methods that connect generated text to supporting evidence. Its joint treatment of attribution, citation, and quotation provides a useful scope beyond conventional RAG surveys.

The collection of 134 papers offers substantial breadth. Citation modality, evidence granularity, visibility, and presentation style are useful organizing dimensions, and the framework and benchmark tables provide accessible entry points into the literature.

The methodology reports research questions, a search string, nine literature sources, inclusion criteria, and independent screening by two authors. Distinguishing evidential support from factual correctness is also conceptually valuable.
weaknesses: The central quantitative contribution is insufficiently reproducible. Sections 1 and 6.3 promise a public Git repository, but the manuscript supplies no repository URL. The complete paper-level annotations, 300-metric inventory, and 231-dataset inventory are absent from the appendices. Metric identity and deduplication rules are unspecified, so readers cannot establish whether the headline totals represent substantively distinct measures or naming and implementation variants.

Several technical inaccuracies directly undermine the evaluation taxonomy. Section 6.1 defines inference-based evaluation as NLI, yet Section 6.2 classifies perplexity under this category; perplexity measures predictive likelihood, not entailment. MAUVE compares distributions of generated and reference text rather than directly measuring fluency and coherence through semantic similarity. The description of FActScore as using human annotation or an NLI model omits its central retrieval-assisted language-model evaluation. Preservation is attributed to a post-retrieval setting even though the cited RARR method is correctly described earlier as post-generation.

The attribution taxonomy needs clearer operational boundaries. Parametric versus non-parametric is defined by access to external evidence at inference, whereas model-centric and data-centric subclasses describe training interventions that can also apply to externally grounded systems. The examples do not establish why these interventions belong specifically under parametric attribution. Similarly, the distinction between attribution and citation evaluation partly follows evaluator choice rather than a clean separation of constructs: citation precision and recall assessed with NLI are placed under attribution. Explicit coding rules and worked examples are needed.

The comprehensive-coverage claim exceeds the search validation provided. Searching titles and abstracts only for the stated terms can miss work using variants such as attributed, grounding, provenance, or quotation; stemming, database-specific query behavior, citation chasing, and recall checks are not documented. The February 2025 cutoff also limits its currency for ACL 2026. Coverage limitations should be analyzed and the search updated or the claims narrowed.

Annotation reliability is not established for the taxonomy underlying the frequency analyses. Although screening was independent, categorization was split between authors, with no reported overlap sample, agreement assessment, or detailed adjudication record. Some distinctions particularly need clarification: quotation terminology appears in 13% of papers, but only one paper receives the quote presentation label.

The synthesis is predominantly descriptive. Frequency counts support observations about the sampled literature, but do not establish methodological superiority, metric validity, or architectural limitations such as the claim that parametric approaches are often unable to provide multiple citations. More critical comparison of methods and evaluator failure modes would strengthen the broader contribution. Overall, the missing audit trail and substantive classification errors prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present; these are concrete revision needs rather than a lack of subjective novelty.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: organizing research on generation with explicit supporting evidence. Bringing attribution, citation, and quotation into one survey is useful, and the contribution appropriately extends beyond retrieval-augmented generation.

The survey provides substantial breadth, covering 134 publications and organizing methods, citation characteristics, tasks, evaluation metrics, and datasets. Figures 4 and 7 and the resource tables offer accessible entry points into the literature.

The methodology reports a search string, nine literature sources, a search cutoff, explicit inclusion criteria, and independent screening by two authors. These are meaningful foundations for a systematic mapping study.

The distinction between evidential support and factual correctness is valuable. The discussion also identifies relevant research directions concerning evaluation standardization and explanations of citation selection.
weaknesses: The evaluation taxonomy contains substantive technical inaccuracies. Section 6.1 defines inference-based evaluation as NLI, but Section 6.2 and Figure 7 classify perplexity under that category; perplexity measures predictive likelihood, not entailment. MAUVE is described as a semantic-similarity measure of fluency and coherence, obscuring its comparison of generated and reference text distributions. FActScore's automated verification is described as NLI rather than its retrieval-supported language-model estimation. These errors affect a central contribution and require a systematic audit of the metric descriptions and assignments.

The attribution taxonomy mixes different axes without sufficiently clear assignment rules. Parametric versus non-parametric is defined by access to external evidence at inference, whereas data-centric versus model-centric concerns how a system is developed. Data or objective changes can also train systems that consume external evidence. Placing preference optimization and FRONT under parametric attribution therefore needs explicit justification based on their inference settings. Likewise, the preservation discussion calls RARR's setting post-retrieval, although Section 5.1.2 correctly presents RARR under post-generation. These inconsistencies weaken confidence in the category counts.

The headline quantitative findings are insufficiently reproducible from the submission. The paper repeatedly mentions a public Git repository but supplies no identifiable repository address. The appendix provides only contribution-type definitions and framework/benchmark tables, rather than the full study-level annotations, metric inventory, or dataset inventory. The rule for counting 300 'distinct metrics' is especially important: precision/recall variants, judge implementations, and custom human criteria could produce very different totals depending on normalization. Without the inventory and counting rules, the evidence for evaluation fragmentation cannot be adequately audited.

Annotation reliability is underdocumented. Although inclusion screening was independent, the substantive categorization was split between the two authors, with regular reviews but no reported overlap audit, agreement measurement, or detailed decision rules for ambiguous cases. This matters because the principal findings depend on interpretive distinctions among attribution approaches, evaluation dimensions, and metric implementations.

The claim to comprehensively map the field exceeds the demonstrated search coverage. The title/abstract query requires 'large language model' or 'llm' together with 'citation', 'attribution', or 'quote'; database-specific stemming, query adaptations, and coverage checks are not reported. Relevant terminology such as grounded generation or attributed question answering may be missed unless the specified terms also appear. There is no reported citation snowballing or recall validation against a known reference set. The February 2025 cutoff is transparent, but also limits the survey's currency for ACL 2026.

The synthesis largely catalogs categories and frequencies rather than critically comparing what existing approaches achieve, where evaluation proxies fail, or which benchmarks support particular conclusions. Low reuse within this selected corpus is suggestive but does not by itself establish field-wide lack of standardization, especially for recently introduced resources. My recommendation is resubmission next cycle: the topic and organization are worthwhile, but technical corrections and an auditable annotation release are needed to establish the soundness and reproducibility required for Findings.

strengths: The topic is highly relevant to NLP: connecting generated claims to evidence is important for evaluating and improving LLM reliability. Jointly examining attribution, citation, and quotation provides a useful organizing perspective.

The survey represents substantial collection effort, covering 134 papers and organizing methods, citation characteristics, evaluation metrics, datasets, and benchmarks. The resource tables and taxonomy figures offer accessible entry points into the literature.

The methodology specifies research questions, a search string, nine literature sources, inclusion criteria, and independent screening by two authors. These are useful foundations for a systematic mapping study.

The distinction between evidential support and factual correctness is valuable. The discussion of evidence granularity, citation visibility, and limited evaluation-framework reuse also identifies practically relevant issues.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient for the central quantitative contribution. Sections 1 and 6.3 refer to a public Git repository, but the manuscript provides no URL. The complete paper-level annotations, metric inventory, and dataset inventory are absent from the appendix. Without these, readers cannot audit the claimed 300 distinct metrics and 231 datasets or reproduce their frequencies. The paper also needs operational rules for merging metric variants and dataset variants.

The evaluation taxonomy contains substantive technical errors. Section 6.1 defines inference-based evaluation through NLI, but Section 6.2 and Figure 7 classify perplexity as inference-based; perplexity measures predictive likelihood, not entailment. MAUVE measures divergence between text distributions rather than the reference-based semantic similarity described here. Preservation is assigned to post-retrieval attribution despite RARR being correctly described earlier as post-generation attribution. These errors affect a principal contribution and warrant a systematic audit.

The attribution taxonomy mixes different classification axes without sufficiently explaining their relationship. Parametric subcategories concern training or data interventions, while non-parametric subcategories concern evidence access and retrieval timing; training interventions can also apply to systems using external evidence. The data-centric category is additionally described as not changing internal behavior, although its examples include preference optimization and supervised training. More explicit decision rules and worked classifications are needed to establish consistent boundaries.

The systematic search does not establish the claimed comprehensiveness. Matching only 'large language model'/'llm' and 'citation'/'attribution'/'quote' in titles and abstracts risks missing related wording and relevant papers without those terms. No citation snowballing or search-recall validation is reported. Categorization was split between annotators, with no reported agreement assessment or independent audit. The February 2025 cutoff also limits the survey's currency for ACL 2026.

Some central counts need reconciliation. Figure 6 reports only one paper using direct quotations, despite the manuscript's discussion of GopherCite and other quote-based approaches; the boundary between quotations and displayed passages needs explicit justification. More generally, the discussion largely extrapolates from frequency counts, offering limited comparative analysis of method tradeoffs or metric validity. The promising synthesis therefore needs corrected classifications and auditable evidence before a sound Findings recommendation; these appear addressable in a next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: organizing research on verifiable generation across attribution, citation, and quotation. Its scope extends usefully beyond conventional RAG surveys.
The substantial literature inventory, multidimensional taxonomy, paper-level annotation tables, and evaluation-resource summaries could provide a valuable reference for researchers.

The methodology includes explicit search and inclusion criteria, a PRISMA flow diagram, a search sensitivity analysis, and independent annotation checks. These provide meaningful evidence of methodological care.
The presentation is generally clear, and the separation of evidence modality, granularity, presentation, and task helps expose design choices that are often discussed separately.
weaknesses: The central evaluation guidelines conflate evaluation targets with evidence availability. Table 1 allows gold-source matching to replace attribution assessment, although matching a gold source does not establish that it supports the generated claim. Table 9 explicitly acknowledges this limitation, contradicting the recommendation. Citation support and completeness can also be evaluated without gold citation sets, as illustrated by ALCE. These distinctions need correction before the guidelines are reliable.

Several metric descriptions are technically inaccurate. Perplexity is classified as inference-based despite that category being defined through natural language inference. Table 9 incorrectly states that FActScore requires a pretrained NLI model, evidence supplied during generation, and typically human atomic-fact decomposition; its automated implementation uses retrieved evidence and automated decomposition and verification. The statement that Citation NLI cannot assess uncited claims also overlooks their treatment in citation recall. These errors affect a principal contribution.

Attribution categories are applied inconsistently. Appendix D classifies PURR as post-retrieval because retrieval precedes revision, while classifying RARR as post-generation despite the same initial-generation, retrieval, and revision structure. Training citation behavior is also insufficient by itself to establish attribution to parametric knowledge. Clear operational rules and an audit of assignments are needed before category frequencies can support the conclusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript: both dataset links terminate at https://github.com/. The complete inventory of 300 metrics and 231 datasets is deferred to this unavailable resource, and metric normalization and distinctness rules are insufficiently specified. Table 7 provides useful partial documentation but cannot reproduce all headline analyses.

Coverage claims exceed the search evidence. The sensitivity analysis finds five eligible papers but excludes them because they do not change the taxonomy, although they could change frequencies and resource inventories. Finding approximately 4% additional papers through one restricted expansion does not establish high overall recall. The February 2025 cutoff also limits claims about the current landscape for ACL 2026.

Reliability checks leave important parts of the contribution unvalidated: taxonomy agreement excludes infrequent labels, contains no parametric-attribution examples, and does not report agreement for metric extraction or evaluation categorization. Frequency-based observations also sometimes become unsupported explanations of effectiveness, scalability, or technical difficulty. The contribution is promising, but the conceptual corrections and reproducibility work are substantial enough to warrant revision before Findings acceptance.

strengths: The topic is highly relevant to NLP: organizing evidence-linked generation across attribution, citation, and quotation could help researchers navigate fragmented terminology and evaluation practices.

The survey provides substantial descriptive coverage: 134 papers, a multidimensional taxonomy, paper-level annotations, and extensive appendices covering methods and evaluation resources. Distinguishing evidence modality, granularity, presentation, and visibility is useful.

The methodology includes explicit search queries, inclusion criteria, a screening flowchart, a sensitivity analysis, and inter-annotator agreement measurements. These are meaningful efforts toward a systematic and reproducible survey.

The manuscript is generally readable, and Table 9 usefully acknowledges limitations of overlap metrics and gold-source matching. The survey appropriately recognizes that factual correctness and evidential support are different properties.
weaknesses: The central evaluation guidance makes an insufficiently justified distinction between attribution and citation. Table 1 recommends choosing between them based on whether gold evidence annotations exist, yet citation support and completeness can be assessed against cited documents without gold citation sets. Conversely, matching gold sources does not establish that those sources support the generated claims, as Table 9 itself acknowledges. Treating citation matching as a possible replacement for attribution evaluation can therefore miss unsupported claims.

Several metric descriptions are technically inaccurate. Section 5.2 classifies perplexity as inference-based, although Section 5.1 explicitly defines that category through natural language inference. Table 9 says FActScore requires a pretrained NLI model and typically human atomic-fact decomposition, overlooking its automated decomposition and retrieval-assisted verification implementations. It also states that Citation NLI cannot assess uncited claims, although ALCE citation recall penalizes missing support, including sentences without citations. These errors affect a principal contribution and require a systematic audit.

The attribution taxonomy needs clearer operational boundaries. Training on attribution data does not by itself make an approach parametric: the relevant question is whether evidence comes from model parameters or external context at inference. Moreover, Appendix D classifies PURR as post-retrieval because evidence precedes its revision, while classifying RARR as post-generation despite a similar generate–retrieve–revise structure. Allowing multiple labels does not resolve inconsistent criteria for assigning them.

Reproducibility of the headline resource analysis remains incomplete. Both repository references resolve only to https://github.com/, while the complete 300-metric inventory and dataset annotations are deferred to that repository. The supplied manuscript therefore does not permit auditing those counts or their mappings to papers. Rules for distinguishing genuinely different metrics from renamed variants or study-specific implementations also need clarification. Reported annotation agreement excludes rare labels and covers neither parametric attribution nor the central metric classification.

Coverage claims exceed what the search validation establishes. Appendix B identifies five additional eligible papers but excludes them because they do not change the taxonomy; that is insufficient justification when the paper also estimates frequencies and trends. Finding approximately 4% additional papers through one alternative query over two sources does not establish near-complete recall. The February 2025 cutoff also limits claims about the current landscape for ACL 2026.

Several interpretations turn prevalence into evidence of effectiveness or causation: post-retrieval popularity is attributed to practical effectiveness, prompting is called state of the art, and sparse parametric work is attributed to technical difficulty and scalability limitations. Publication counts alone do not establish these conclusions. Overall, the survey has a useful foundation, but the evaluation errors, inconsistent classification rules, and incomplete auditability prevent a sound Findings recommendation in its present form; these appear addressable in a next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: organizing research on explicitly linking generated text to supporting evidence. Its joint treatment of attribution, citations, and quotations provides a useful perspective beyond general RAG and hallucination surveys.

The multidimensional taxonomy separates attribution approaches, citation characteristics, and tasks. Distinctions concerning evidence granularity, citation visibility, and presentation are useful for comparing heterogeneous systems.

The survey provides substantial descriptive coverage through 134 annotated papers and extensive resource tables. Its methodology includes explicit search and inclusion criteria, a PRISMA flow diagram, a sensitivity analysis, and reported inter-annotator agreement. These are meaningful strengths for a survey contribution.

The organization is generally clear, and the discussion highlights relevant research questions concerning multimodal evidence, hybrid attribution, and evaluation standardization. Table 9 usefully acknowledges limitations of lexical similarity and gold-source matching.
weaknesses: The evaluation catalogue, a central contribution, contains substantive technical inaccuracies. Section 5.2 classifies perplexity as inference-based although Section 5.1 defines that category specifically through NLI entailment. Table 9 incorrectly describes FActScore as requiring a pretrained NLI model and typically human atomic-fact decomposition; its automated implementation uses language-model-based decomposition and verification. The statement that Citation NLI cannot assess uncited claims also overlooks how citation recall penalizes unsupported or uncited sentences. These errors require a systematic audit of metric descriptions and assignments.

The evaluation guidelines conflate the property being evaluated with the availability of gold annotations. Table 1 recommends attribution when gold evidence is unavailable and permits citation evaluation instead when it is available. However, matching a gold source set and verifying that the actually cited passages support generated claims are distinct requirements. Table 9 itself acknowledges that citation retrieval matching does not establish claim support. The proposed substitution can therefore leave a central aspect of citation quality untested.

Attribution categories need more consistent operational boundaries. Appendix D classifies PURR as post-retrieval because retrieved evidence precedes its revision, while classifying RARR as post-generation despite both starting from an existing response and retrieving evidence for revision. Similarly, the parametric model/data-centric categories need to distinguish training a citation-capable model from attributing knowledge stored in its parameters. Allowing multiple labels is reasonable, but does not resolve inconsistent decision rules; the resulting prevalence statistics depend on these decisions.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Both repository references terminate at https://github.com/, leaving the full 300-metric catalogue and 231-dataset inventory inaccessible. The paper also needs explicit metric deduplication rules to substantiate the claim of 300 distinct metrics. Reported annotation agreement does not cover metric classifications, excludes rare labels, and includes no parametric-attribution examples, limiting validation of several central analyses.

Coverage conclusions exceed what the search establishes. The sensitivity search found five eligible additional papers but deliberately excluded them because they did not alter the taxonomy; this does not justify excluding them from frequency and resource analyses. Finding few papers with one additional query also does not establish high recall. The February 2025 cutoff limits claims about the current ACL 2026 research landscape, and statements that prevalence demonstrates practical effectiveness or that prompting is state of the art are not established by publication counts.

Overall, the survey has clear potential, but the metric inaccuracies, classification inconsistencies, and incomplete audit trail prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present. These are substantive but tractable revisions, supporting resubmission next cycle rather than rejection of the survey's aims or relevance.
